Garden teaching case · Stage four

Temporal Projection Integrity Engine

Will puddle water reach the stream during the next rain? Will tonight’s roof dew reach the garden by morning? The Lattice Atlas supplies a possible route for each claim. This record tests how far the evidence supports either prediction.

What the two snapshots establish

The first snapshot contains sixteen written connections. The second preserves those and extends the register to thirty-six. Their sequence dates additions to the description. Neither snapshot records a visit, a rain event, a temperature reading or a measured transfer of water. Factual strength for the two predictions remains unscored.

What the yard location changes

The Atlas locates the starting puddle in the yard. The household discovery and puddle location are established for the example and contain no prediction. The reports include no rain event, runoff observation, barrel discharge or household action. Neither forecast gains evidential support from either statement.

Classification checks in order

Classification four · Projected — mechanism-grounded
The register describes runoff, condensation and collection. Neither claim identifies prospective harm or documents a mechanism actively producing it in this garden. There is no independent evidence of its output in comparable conditions or measurement placing this garden within those conditions. All three evidence requirements would need factual strength of at least seven. Neither claim qualifies.
Classification one · Projected — evidence-grounded
Neither route has measured directional change across two garden observations. A one-step continuation would require documented change, founding evidence with factual strength of at least seven, and no intervening variable.
Classification two · Projected — conditional
Rainfall alone leaves the puddle’s connection to the stream unknown. Dew formation alone leaves the hose outlet and operation unknown. Neither route has a field snapshot establishing a pattern with factual strength from five through six point nine. Naming a condition supplies no measurement of its probability.
Classification three · Inference — excluded
Both predictions depend on unobserved local conditions. Each remains an open lead. The supported forward distance is zero for both.

Open leads

One · Puddle water will reach the stream during the next rain

Basis. Entry 005 takes puddle water downhill. Entry 033 carries runoff into the stream. Entries 004, 008, 031 and 032 describe another possible arrival through groundwater. A stream reading by itself would leave the water’s origin open.

Classification three · Inference — excluded. Snapshot basis for the route description is the first written snapshot and the expanded written snapshot. Field snapshot basis for the prediction is absent. Grounding is insufficient for a forward observation.

What would reopen it. If the surface route is tested during rain, record when water leaves the yard puddle, where the downhill flow connects or stops, and whether it reaches the stream bank. Append that event to the evidence register with references to entries 5 and 33. A continuously observed connection to the stream establishes that surface transfer for that event. If flow stops, record the observed endpoint. A gap in observation leaves the connection unverified.

Two · Tonight’s roof dew will reach garden soil by morning

Basis. Entries 027 through 030 connect roof dew, gutter, barrel and hose. Entry 030 leaves the timing of delivery open. Water already held in the barrel could also supply the hose.

Classification three · Inference — excluded. The expanded written snapshot contains the route. Field snapshot basis for the prediction is absent. Grounding is insufficient for a forward observation.

What would reopen it. If this overnight route is tested, record the starting barrel contents, roof and gutter inflow, other water sources and hose discharge at the garden outlet before morning. Append the event to the evidence register against entries 27 through 30. The route is established for that night only if the delivered water can be traced to the roof dew. If the source mixes with other water and cannot be distinguished, record collection and discharge separately.

Could a hose discharge directly into the puddle?

This is a comparison of possible endpoints. Neither follow-up reports hose use. If a direct hose arrival is later reported, the lead investigator would append the account to the evidence register, separate from entry 30. It would need to identify the water source feeding the hose and trace the same continuous discharge from that source through the outlet into the original yard puddle. An observation ending at garden soil supports only that endpoint. An interrupted or unseen connection leaves the puddle arrival unverified.

A continuous source-to-puddle observation would settle that transfer for the observed event. Attributing the action to the household would require a source that separately establishes who operated the hose and their connection to the household. The example contains no such attribution. See how that affects the notice decision.

Decision

Zero forward observations advance. Both open leads retain their original entry references so a later observation can be checked against the specific transfer it supports.
